rv.q: I'd give it a few more days before you go, but it's already the kind of show — clever, unpredictable new work with promise! — to which the city's theater should make haste to return.
Overall, the strong performances by Odom, Gonzalez-Cadel and Audrey Billings make the play worth seeing. But the distracting narration and Twilight Zone absurdity make the plot difficult to follow.

The result is like a Harold Pinter play filtered through the lens of our national fetish for instant gratification and individualism, with a dollop of late-capitalist assumptions about the value of human life.
Come ready to think and be prepared to leave wishing for more new works like this one: ingenious, thoughtful, and unafraid.
The performances are finely wrought, it's staged with fleet and captivating brio, and the visual and design elements are all clean and sharp.
THINGS WITH FRIENDS, filled with fast-paced dialogue, will amuse, astonish and possibly even astound or anger some audience members.
This is theatre that's ferociously alive. This is theatre.
After the initial exchange of histrionic gestures of affection, it quickly becomes clear that, if guests Chabby and Vy are friends, their hosts need no enemies.

It’s a surrealist, climate anxiety comedy of errors that takes place over one wild dinner party. At the show’s conclusion one walks away with some vague anti-commercialist messaging, but also more than a few questions, or just one in particular: Why did I let myself suffer through that?

The other couple, Vy (a powerful performance by Cruz Gonzalez-Cadel) and her husband, Chabby ( Jon Hudson Odom in what I might call a break out comedic character with evil intentions). It turns out that each of these couples has a different idea of what their relationship was, is, and might become.
